newsitem.title: USA: Actor Anthony Quinn, wife reach divorce settlement.
newsitem.headline: Actor Anthony Quinn, wife reach divorce settlement.

text.p: Actor Anthony Quinn and his estranged wife reached a private divorce settlement on Tuesday, a day after their son testified the Hollywood star beat his mother if she mentioned his infidelity.
Terms of the settlement, which ended what promised to be a nasty divorce battle, were not released, said a spokesman for Iolanda Quinn's attorney, Raoul Felder.
"Mr. Quinn signed an agreement at about 2 a.m.," said the spokesman. "Mrs. Quinn is very happy."

Testimony in the case began on Monday in a Manhattan courtroom, where the 82-year-old, two-time Academy Award winner and his second wife, Italian-born Iolanda Quinn, 62, were fighting over a reported $20 million in assets.
Their son, Danny Quinn, 33, also an actor, said his father would hit his mother if she brought up his extramarital affairs.
"He'd say, 'Be quiet. Shut up,'" he said. "Then he'd throw something -- dishes, breakable glass -- at her, and sometimes he would hit her on the arm.
"She'd come back to the room with dark bruises on her arm," the son said.
The actor has 13 legitimate and illegitimate children, Felder said.
The silver-haired actor left Iolanda for his 35-year-old former secretary, Kathy Benvin, several years ago. They have two children, Antonia, 4, and Ryan, 1.

Quinn's oldest son, Francesco, had been scheduled to testify on Tuesday about physical confrontations with his father, Felder said. That testimony would have been just as "devastating" to Quinn, the attorney claimed.
"He (Quinn) knew what was coming down the pike. The other son was going to testify," Felder said. "We did very well ... She's satisfied with the money."
Terms of the settlement were secret at the actor's request, Felder said. He did say it was "a fair assumption" that she got at least half his assets.
The Quinns had a prenuptual agreement from 1965 that limited her to about one-eighth of their community property.
But she said she wanted an equitable settlement and more than half of her husband's homes, art, antiques and investments.
The art collection was a sticking point in negotiations, the actor said outside court on Monday.

"I want to save my art, all the art that I acquired in my life," he said. His collection included works by Pablo Picasso, Alexander Calder, Henry Moore and Henri Matisse, his attorney Barry Slotnick said.
